Never trust a map

All of them are dirty liars.

All maps lie. Some lie more than others, and some are deliberately designed to mislead us. Mark Monmonier wrote a whole book about it. How to Lie with Maps

Take election maps. Land doesn’t vote. People do. Yet a vast, sparsely populated region can dominate a map, while a densely populated city barely gets noticed. See the same election mapped several ways

Change the color scale or the class breaks on a choropleth and the same data can tell a very different story. See what changing the class breaks does

But even the most honest maps lie.

The Earth is (approximately) a sphere, and there’s no way to flatten it without distorting something. A projection can preserve some properties, such as area or local angles, at the expense of others.

Fortunately, we have a lie detector.

Meet Tissot’s indicatrices

Imagine placing tiny, identical circles all over the globe. Flatten the globe and those circles can change size, shape or both. The area of each ellipse shows how much the projection enlarges or shrinks the area there. Its shape shows whether the projection stretches more in one direction than another.

A quick technical note

Strictly speaking, Tissot’s indicatrices describe what happens to infinitesimally small circles. The geom_tissot() function in crstools takes a practical approach. It draws geographic buffers around the grid points and projects them along with the rest of the map.

That gives us a visual approximation. For point-by-point measurements, the tissot package calculates local distortion factors with PROJ. We’re here to make maps, so the buffers will do nicely.

Let’s put some maps to the test.

Same circles, different maps

We’ll start with the same grid for all twelve projections. At each of its 49 crossings, we’ll draw a circle with a radius of 500 km. In Goode, we skip circles that straddle a cut. In the orthographic view, we draw only those that fit entirely on the visible side of the globe.

In R, we get country boundaries from giscoR, build the grid with sf and draw the maps with ggplot2 and crstools.

Web Mercator

If the circles are still circles, where’s the lie?

Compare the middle row with the top and bottom rows. The circles stay roughly round, but they take up much more room at high latitudes. That’s how Greenland gets to look so big.

How we drew it

Show the R code

The first block loads Inter Tight for all the map titles and sets up the projections, country boundaries and grid. The second draws the maps and handles Goode’s cuts and the orthographic horizon.

map_family <- "inter-tight"
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_family)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()
library(crstools)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

meridians <- seq(-150, 150, 50)
parallels <- seq(-75, 75, 25)
earth_radius <- 6371007.181
buffer_km <- 500
map_background <- "grey90"

projections <- c(
  setNames("EPSG:4326", "Plate carr\u00e9e"),
  "Web Mercator" = "EPSG:3857",
  "Robinson" = "+proj=robin",
  "Winkel Tripel" = "+proj=wintri",
  "Mollweide" = "ESRI:54009",
  "Sinusoidal" = "ESRI:54008",
  "Equal Earth" = "+proj=eqearth +datum=WGS84",
  "Hammer" = "+proj=hammer +R=6371007.181",
  "Bonne" = "ESRI:54024",
  "Goode homolosine" = "+proj=igh +R=6371007.181",
  "Van der Grinten" = "ESRI:54029",
  "Orthographic" = "+proj=ortho +lat_0=30 +lon_0=10 +R=6371007.181"
)

frame <- st_linestring(rbind(
  c(-175, 85),
  c(175, 85),
  c(175, -85),
  c(-175, -85),
  c(-175, 85)
)) |>
  st_segmentize(5) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  st_sfc(crs = 4326)

world <- giscoR::gisco_get_countries(epsg = 4326, resolution = 10)
graticule <- st_graticule(frame, lon = meridians, lat = parallels)

goode_lat <- c(90:-90, rep(c(-90:0, 0:-90), 3), -90:90, 90:0, 0:90, 90)
goode_lon <- c(
  rep(180, 181),
  rep(c(80.01, 79.99, -19.99, -20.01, -99.99, -100.01), each = 91),
  rep(-180, 181),
  rep(c(-40.01, -39.99), each = 91),
  180
)
goode_frame <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(cbind(goode_lon, goode_lat))), crs = 4326)

goode_lobes <- rbind(
  c(-180, -40, 0, 90),
  c(-40, 180, 0, 90),
  c(-180, -100, -90, 0),
  c(-100, -20, -90, 0),
  c(-20, 80, -90, 0),
  c(80, 180, -90, 0)
)

goode_lines <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(goode_lobes)), function(index) {
  bounds <- goode_lobes[index, ]
  longitude <- seq(bounds[1] + 0.01, bounds[2] - 0.01, length.out = 361)
  latitude <- seq(bounds[3] + 0.01, bounds[4] - 0.01, length.out = 181)
  lng <- meridians[meridians > bounds[1] & meridians < bounds[2]]
  lat <- parallels[parallels > bounds[3] & parallels < bounds[4]]
  c(
    lapply(lng, function(x) st_linestring(cbind(x, latitude))),
    lapply(lat, function(y) st_linestring(cbind(longitude, y)))
  )
})
goode_grid <- st_sfc(
  c(
    list(st_linestring(cbind(seq(-179.99, 179.99, length.out = 721), 0))),
    do.call(c, goode_lines)
  ),
  crs = 4326
)
indicatrices <- function(lng, lat) {
  geom_tissot(
    data = world,
    radius = units::as_units(buffer_km, "km"),
    fill = "#E63946",
    color = "#A4161A",
    alpha = 0.65,
    centres = list(lng = lng, lat = lat)
  )
}

draw_map <- function(title) {
  projection <- projections[[title]]
  grid <- graticule
  circles <- indicatrices(meridians, parallels)
  land <- st_geometry(world)
  radians <- pi / 180
  buffer_limit <- sin(buffer_km * 1000 / earth_radius)

  if (title == "Goode homolosine") {
    outline <- st_transform(goode_frame, projection)
    grid <- st_transform(goode_grid, projection)
    circles <- lapply(parallels, function(lat) {
      cuts <- if (lat > 0) -40 else c(-100, -20, 80)
      longitude_gap <- abs((outer(meridians, cuts, "-") + 180) %% 360 - 180)
      distance <- sin(pmin(longitude_gap, 90) * radians) * cos(lat * radians)
      visible <- meridians[apply(distance, 1, min) > buffer_limit]
      indicatrices(visible, lat)
    })
  } else if (title == "Orthographic") {
    outline <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 0)), crs = projection) |>
      st_buffer(earth_radius, nQuadSegs = 180)

    # Clip land just inside the horizon in a distance-preserving projection.
    distance_crs <- sub("+proj=ortho", "+proj=aeqd", projection, fixed = TRUE)
    hemisphere <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 0)), crs = distance_crs) |>
      st_buffer(pi * earth_radius / 2 - 1, nQuadSegs = 180)
    land <- st_transform(land, distance_crs, partial = TRUE) |>
      st_make_valid() |>
      st_intersection(hemisphere)

    # Keep circles whose entire buffer fits on the visible hemisphere.
    circles <- lapply(parallels, function(lat) {
      cosine <- sin(lat * radians) * sin(30 * radians) +
        cos(lat * radians) * cos(30 * radians) *
          cos((meridians - 10) * radians)
      visible <- meridians[cosine > buffer_limit]
      if (length(visible)) indicatrices(visible, lat)
    })
    # All meridians meet at the pole, so draw one circle there.
    circles <- c(circles, list(indicatrices(10, 90)))
  } else {
    outline <- st_transform(frame, projection, partial = TRUE)
  }

  limits <- st_bbox(outline)
  land <- st_transform(land, projection, partial = TRUE)
  if (st_is_longlat(land)) {
    # Clip the longitude-latitude panel in its display coordinates.
    land <- st_set_crs(land, NA) |>
      st_make_valid() |>
      st_intersection(st_set_crs(outline, NA)) |>
      st_set_crs(projection)
  } else {
    land <- st_intersection(st_make_valid(land), st_make_valid(outline))
  }

  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = outline, fill = "white", color = NA) +
    geom_sf(data = land, fill = "grey70", color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15) +
    geom_sf(
      data = grid,
      color = "grey40",
      alpha = 0.45,
      linewidth = 0.3
    ) +
    geom_sf(data = outline, fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.75) +
    circles +
    coord_sf(
      crs = projection,
      xlim = limits[c("xmin", "xmax")],
      ylim = limits[c("ymin", "ymax")],
      datum = NA
    ) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void(base_family = map_family) +
    theme(
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = map_background, color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = map_background, color = NA)
    )
}

Equal Earth

Let’s see what happens when we make area the one thing the map has to get right.

draw_map("Equal Earth")

The shapes give the game away. The circles flatten toward the top and bottom, but their areas stay roughly the same. Greenland can keep its place on the map without borrowing space from the tropics.

Winkel Tripel

What if we spread the distortion around? Winkel Tripel is a compromise projection. Follow the 50° N row from the central meridian toward either edge and watch the ellipses stretch and tilt. Compare them with the equatorial row and you’ll see their areas change too.

draw_map("Winkel Tripel")

What if we cut the map?

The interrupted Goode homolosine projection preserves area. It also splits the world into lobes, which helps keep shapes closer to what we’d see on a globe. Imagine dropping our red circles onto the pieces of an orange peel. A circle that straddles a cut would show up in two pieces, so we leave it out of the gallery. Let’s peel the world

Twelve ways to flatten the world

  • Conformal. These projections preserve local angles and shapes, so tiny circles stay round even when their size changes. Mercator is useful for navigation because a constant compass bearing follows a straight line.
  • Equal-area. These projections keep areas in proportion, even when shapes stretch. Equal Earth works well for thematic world maps, where readers may want to compare how much land different regions or categories cover.
  • Compromise. These projections balance different kinds of distortion. Both area and shape can change. Robinson and Winkel Tripel are useful for general-purpose world maps and atlases, where the overall view matters.

Find the red circle over Greenland and follow it from map to map. The orthographic view, centered over North Africa, looks like a globe from space. It shows only the circles that fit entirely on the visible side, including a bonus circle at the North Pole. Each map is scaled to fit its panel, so compare the shapes and relative sizes of the red circles within each map.

featured <- c("Web Mercator", "Equal Earth", "Winkel Tripel")
gallery_order <- c(featured, setdiff(names(projections), featured))

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = map_background, col = NA))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
  width = 0.96,
  height = 0.96,
  layout = grid::grid.layout(
    6, 3,
    heights = grid::unit(c(2, 1.5, 10, 10, 10, 10), "null")
  )
))
grid::grid.text(
  "One Earth, twelve projections",
  gp = grid::gpar(
    fontfamily = map_family, fontsize = 25, fontface = "bold", col = "grey15"
  ),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1:3)
)
grid::grid.text(
  "Each red shape starts as a circle with a radius of 500 km",
  gp = grid::gpar(fontfamily = map_family, fontsize = 14, col = "grey25"),
  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1:3)
)

for (index in seq_along(gallery_order)) {
  title <- gallery_order[[index]]
  grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(
    layout.pos.row = (index - 1) %/% 3 + 3,
    layout.pos.col = (index - 1) %% 3 + 1,
    layout = grid::grid.layout(2, 1, heights = grid::unit(c(1, 9), "null"))
  ))
  grid::grid.text(
    title,
    gp = grid::gpar(
      fontfamily = map_family, fontsize = 14, fontface = "bold", col = "grey15"
    ),
    vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1)
  )
  grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2))
  map <- draw_map(title) + theme(plot.title = element_blank())
  print(map, vp = grid::viewport(width = 0.94, height = 0.94))
  grid::popViewport(2)
}
grid::popViewport()

So, which map should you trust? Depends on what you’re asking it to show.
